primary_claim: Across seven identified failure modes of AI truth-seeking, the authors developed evaluation metrics validated against human judgment or ground-truth outcomes for six of them, found very limited transfer between different truth-seeking aspects and domains (near-zero cross-domain correlation, training useless or backfiring OOD about 50% of the time), and identified several effective but mutually incompatible per-aspect interventions (bootstrap-based consistency maximization, reasoning-coverage RL, RL on Brier reward).

effect.metric: correlation with human judgment (rho) for LLM-based judges; cross-aspect/cross-domain transfer correlation
effect.value: debate-based judge achieves rho=0.595 with human annotation on conceptual-deconfusion-type failure modes; near-zero correlation between accuracy on different domains (e.g. forecasting vs academic review); training on one aspect/domain useless or backfires OOD roughly 50% of the time

stated_future_work: Open-source experimental infrastructure coming soon in the same sequence.
limitations_stated: This study is for stage-setting purposes and shouldn't be seen as conclusive.

The verifiability/falsifiability/predictive-power metric failed outright: limited internal agreement between predictor models and zero correlation with the external golden standard (LMArena Elo), likely due to spurious token-level correlations.
Have not applied interpretability techniques to rule out the model having sycophantic hidden thoughts not put into writing during reasoning.
Combined training (reasoning-coverage RL followed by Brier RL) works poorly despite seeming complementary, an unexplained empirical incompatibility.
quote: We see very limited transfer between different aspects. Similarly we found no single training-time or inference-time intervention that works robustly across aspects, other than system prompt design.
